gist: A history of ADSL: how Joe Lechleider's asymmetric-bandwidth insight at Bellcore, the 1993 Bellcore 'ADSL Olympics' line-code shootout won by Amati's Discrete Multitone, and a three-person Alcatel research team in Antwerp turned 1880s-vintage telephone copper into megabit broadband. Built for a failed video-streaming product (Video Dial Tone), ADSL was pivoted to internet access and peaked at roughly 360 million lines worldwide with Alcatel holding 40-50% share.

insights.claim: AT&T's telephone plant was still built on essentially the same twisted-pair copper technology introduced in 1887, giving telecoms an enormous sunk-cost installed base of millions of miles of wire that carried only analog voice for decades.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: The value of an incumbent's legacy physical plant depends entirely on whether a new modulation technology can be retrofitted onto it; retrofit innovations can revalue assets thought to be obsolete.

insights.claim: Roughly 99% of the telephone network's wire measured by length is 'last mile' - runs of one to two miles or less into individual homes - which makes it the least economical portion to replace with fiber, both on capex and because upgrading requires entering the customer's house.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Explains the durable structural bottleneck in all access-network investment cases: the cheapest capital move is always to squeeze more bits out of existing last-mile wire rather than trench new media.

insights.claim: At Alcatel's Antwerp research center, optical fiber measurably outperformed copper and coax but its high unit cost made it impractical for wide deployment, so copper was explicitly treated as the stopgap medium until fiber costs fell - a gap that lasted decades.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: A 'best technology is too expensive today' gap is where the largest interim-technology markets get created; interim does not mean short-lived.

themes.theme: Cable Pressure Creates Video Dial Tone

insights.claim: The 1984 Cable Communications Policy Act deregulated cable TV rates, cable operators immediately raised rates about 60%, and that cash funded national build-outs that grew the number of US cable systems 40% between 1985 and 1990.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: A clean template for how price deregulation converts into infrastructure capex and market-share land grabs - watch for the same pattern in any newly deregulated utility.

insights.claim: The Baby Bells' strategic fear was not cable's video revenue but cable's direct coax relationship with the household, because coax could plausibly be used to deliver telephone calls and disintermediate the telcos - which cable operators eventually did.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Owning the physical connection into the home is the strategic asset; adjacent-service invasion follows from the wire, not the content.

insights.claim: Because antitrust and telecom law barred the Baby Bells from buying cable operators inside their own service areas, and the FCC's mid-1992 ruling let them transmit but not own video content, the telcos were forced into building Video Dial Tone themselves as a common-carrier streaming service for third-party studios.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Regulatory constraints, not customer demand, dictated the product architecture - and a product whose existence depends on a rule is destroyed when the rule changes.

themes.theme: Asymmetry Beats Symmetry on Twisted Pair

insights.claim: ISDN, standardized by Bell Labs from 1980, delivered only two bidirectional 64 kbps channels plus a 16 kbps overhead channel - about 144 kbps total - and was mocked in the industry as 'Innovation Subscribers Don't Need' because it was too slow to be compelling in the US.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: A standard that clears the engineering bar but not the user-value bar fails to be adopted; the marginal speed gain, not the architecture, determines uptake.

insights.claim: The binding physical constraint on faster copper was near-end crosstalk (NEXT), where a transmitting twisted pair electromagnetically couples into a neighboring receiving pair inside the shared cable bundle near the carrier station.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Identifying which physical impairment actually caps a medium is what reveals whether a bottleneck is a hard wall or an engineering choice.

insights.claim: Joe Lechleider's key insight was that the carrier end of the loop is far noisier than the household end because that is where all the twisted pairs bundle together, so the quiet household side can receive far more data than the carrier side can - justifying an asymmetric frequency split rather than the intuitive 50/50 transmit/receive allocation, with the shrunken upstream pushed into lower, less crosstalk-prone frequencies.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: The reusable model: when a channel's noise is spatially asymmetric, allocating capacity asymmetrically extracts far more total throughput than the symmetric default - and it is why consumer broadband download/upload asymmetry is permanent.

insights.claim: Bellcore's 1993 line-code competition - the 'Bellcore ADSL Olympics' or 'Bellcore Shootout' - pitted AT&T's CAP (carrierless amplitude/phase) and Broadcom Corporation's QAM, both single-carrier and battle-tested, against Discrete Multitone from Amati, a startup led by Stanford professor John Cioffi.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: A single standards bake-off reallocated a multi-decade equipment market; standards contests are where incumbent advantage is won or lost.

insights.claim: DMT won the bake-off by splitting the 1.1 MHz of usable copper bandwidth into roughly 256 slices of about 4 kHz each and transmitting QAM-encoded data in parallel across them, delivering about 50% more efficiency and speeds up to four times faster than rivals at 6 megabits per second.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Multi-carrier parallelism, the same principle as OFDM in wireless, was the step change that made copper broadband commercially viable.

insights.claim: DMT's decisive advantage over single-carrier codes was per-loop adaptability: it can probe an individual copper line and vary bits per hertz slice by slice - down to about 4 bits per hertz at attenuated high frequencies - pushing each of millions of heterogeneous loops near its theoretical limit.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: When the deployed base is wildly heterogeneous, an adaptive technology beats a nominally faster fixed one - the same logic that later favored adaptive rate schemes across networking.

insights.claim: DMT's cost was complexity and computational intensity - running 256 parallel channels demanded serious custom silicon - which meant the standard's victory created a new semiconductor requirement that only a vendor willing to build chips could satisfy, since Amati had brought only a prototype.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Standards that demand heavy compute transfer the profit pool to whoever can industrialize the silicon, not to the algorithm's inventor.

insights.claim: Alcatel's ADSL program began from a coffee-break conversation between researchers Martin De Prycker and Willem Verbiest about separate 1990 trips to Bellcore where both had seen a fridge-sized symmetrical broadband DSL prototype running 1.5 Mbps over twisted pair; on that evidence they won approval for a three-person autonomous team with no twisted-pair background that started work in January 1992.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Early ugly prototypes are the leading indicator worth tracking - the strategic signal is feasibility, not form factor - and small autonomous teams without incumbent domain priors are how a legacy switch vendor caught the discontinuity.
insights.quote: but they were smart and that's all that mattered.

insights.claim: Alcatel had been co-developing CAP with Bellcore and was certain CAP would become the standard; Willem Verbiest learned only on returning to Belgium in March 1993 that DMT had won, meaning the team had developed the wrong technology.
insights.speaker: Willem Verbiest (Alcatel researcher, quoted in a case study)
insights.so_what: Co-developing with a standards body is no hedge against losing the standard - concentration risk on a single line code nearly killed the program.

insights.claim: Alcatel's response to losing the line-code bet was to immediately license and adopt DMT despite knowing little about it, explicitly to earn a seat shaping the ADSL standard, and management expanded the team from three to over 100 people on that leap of faith.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Speed of capitulation to a winning standard, plus willingness to fund it before revenue exists, is what separated Alcatel from rivals that defended their own codes.
insights.quote: management took a leap of faith.

insights.claim: Alcatel shipped the first DMT-based ADSL chipset in 1995 - an analog ASIC, a digital signal processor and a channel processor fabbed on a 0.7 micrometer node - less than two years after its pivot and a few months before the ADSL standard was finalized, then demonstrated an end-to-end prototype at the October 1995 Telecom Geneva Fair.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Shipping silicon ahead of standard ratification is the classic way a vendor locks in a share position before the market exists.

insights.claim: Competitors that refused DMT bet wrong: AT&T stayed with CAP and produced chipsets with partner Paradyne, while Nortel - then committed to optical fiber - rejected DMT-based ADSL and pursued a proprietary hybrid called Etherloop, and ultimately every competing variant (HDSL, SDSL, IDSL, RADSL, the whole 'xDSL' zoo) collapsed into ADSL.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Proprietary or fiber-first strategies forfeited the copper broadband decade; standard convergence eventually eliminates the alternatives entirely.
insights.quote: ultimately, xDSL and all others became just ADSL.

insights.claim: Video Dial Tone failed despite a functional product: beta testers reported channel-changing lag under one second and picture and audio quality comparable to broadcast satellite, and Bell Atlantic CEO Ray Smith publicly argued ADSL was not a second-best interim technology.
insights.speaker: Ray Smith (Bell Atlantic CEO, 1995 Wired interview) / Jon Y
insights.so_what: Product quality was never the failure mode - a useful reminder that distribution rights and regulation kill products that demos suggest should win.
insights.quote: You can do the virtual VCR over it.

insights.claim: Ray Smith argued ADSL had better install economics than cable because although per-house cost is higher, the telco only incurs it after a sale is made, whereas cable operators must wire whole neighborhoods where not every home subscribes.
insights.speaker: Ray Smith (Bell Atlantic CEO)
insights.so_what: Success-based capex versus homes-passed capex is still the core comparison in any access-network investment case, including fiber versus fixed wireless today.
insights.quote: but you do it only after the sale is made.

insights.claim: Video Dial Tone's proximate cause of death was content starvation: because the rules barred telcos from owning video content, the business depended on persuading movie studios to lease channels, and many studios simply did not bother.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: A platform that cannot own or guarantee supply is hostage to rights holders - the same dynamic that later forced streaming platforms into originals.

insights.claim: The final blow was regulatory: pre-1996 FCC failure to produce coherent Video Dial Tone rules already caused several carriers to drop support, and the 1996 Telecommunications Act then lifted the in-area cable ownership restriction, obliterating VDT's entire reason to exist and briefly leaving ADSL looking doomed.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Regulatory-arbitrage products carry binary policy risk; the deregulation that seems favorable can destroy the product built to work around the old rule.

insights.claim: By mid-1997 Alcatel had a finished ADSL video-streaming product for customers who no longer wanted it, and only the technical overlap between video and web use - small upstream requests, large downstream deliveries - let the same technology be repurposed for internet access.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: The traffic-profile match, not the original use case, is what made the pivot cheap - a general test for whether a stranded technology can be redeployed.

themes.theme: Dial-Up Pain as the Demand Trigger

insights.claim: Voiceband modems were capped by physics, not products: the voice band grants only about 3.3 kHz of usable frequency, so dial-up topped out at 28.8 kbps during AOL's US boom and 56K modems did not arrive until late 1997.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Quantifies how large the ADSL speed jump was (kilobits to megabits) and why demand was pent up rather than created by marketing.

insights.claim: A Pacific Telesis study of a roughly 24-mile-diameter region, cited in 1996, found 16% of local calls failed to connect due to heavy internet usage versus a historical 1% failure rate, showing dial-up was congesting the voice network itself.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Internet traffic was degrading the telcos' core voice product, giving them a defensive cost reason - not just a growth reason - to fund always-on broadband.
insights.quote: Historically, just 1% of calls fail to connect.

insights.claim: ADSL's decisive consumer advantage over dial-up was that it did not seize the phone line or consume priced voice minutes, removing the household conflict between being online and receiving calls.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: The 'always-on, non-blocking' attribute, more than raw speed, is what converted internet access from a session into a utility.
insights.quote: ADSL did not block the phone.

insights.claim: Even with clear internet demand, the Baby Bell telcos initially refused to follow Alcatel's pivot from video to broadband - scarred by Video Dial Tone's failure and daunted by the operational scale of supporting millions of subscribers.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Incumbent adoption lag after a failed prior initiative is a recurring source of timing risk for equipment vendors, even when end demand is proven.

themes.theme: Procurement Scale to Global DSL Peak

insights.claim: The 1996 Telecom Act's creation of Competitive Local Exchange Carriers, which obligated the Bells to lease their copper lines and equipment to startups reselling to ISPs, was a competitive forcing function that pushed the incumbent Bells into launching their own broadband.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Mandated wholesale access on incumbent infrastructure accelerated retail broadband deployment - the policy lever that later explains Europe's DSL lead.

insights.claim: In August 1996 four Baby Bells - Ameritech, BellSouth, Pacific Bell and SBC Communications, together serving 65% of the US population - formed the Joint Procurement Consortium to buy ADSL gear jointly, and in October 1996 Alcatel won that RFP over Westell and Ericsson on price and on offering a full end-to-end stack from modems to DSLAMs.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: One consortium award covering two-thirds of the US population set the vendor hierarchy for a decade; group purchasing plus standardization was also the explicit lever for crushing per-subscriber CPE cost (in-home splitter and modem plus a central-office DSLAM slot), just as cable had done with cable modems.

insights.claim: US DSL scaled from commercial launch around 1999 to about 2 million subscribers in 2000, nearly doubled the next year, and reached nearly 12 million by 2004 - keeping pace with cable's roughly 15 million.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Benchmarks the adoption curve of a retrofit access technology: roughly five years from launch to eight figures of subscribers once procurement scale exists.

insights.claim: DSL penetrated harder outside the US - Alcatel shipped a million lines by 1999, Singapore's Singtel trialled early before jumping to fiber, Korea passed 10 million users by 2002, and DSL led OECD broadband because European cable was weak and regulators forced incumbents to open lines to DSL-only startups.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Dense apartment housing plus legacy copper plus unbundling regulation is the combination that maximizes copper broadband share - a repeatable screen for access-technology adoption by geography.

insights.claim: DSL lines peaked around 360 million globally in the late 2000s and early 2010s with Alcatel holding 40-50% market share throughout, and later variants such as VDSL2 pushed twisted pair to as much as 200 megabits per second.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Sizes both the total market and the durability of a standards-driven share position; sustained ~45% share of a 360-million-line market is the payoff of winning the standard early.

insights.claim: Legacy access technologies decay far more slowly than headlines suggest: over a hundred million DSL subscribers still get internet over copper, and AOL only finally shut down its dial-up service in September 2025.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Terminal-decline assumptions on legacy telecom assets are routinely too aggressive; residual copper subscriber bases can fund cash flows for many more years.
